items.question: Explain in your own words WHY the gap between simple and compound grows over time.
items.expectedAnswer: Under simple interest, every year's interest is calculated on the ORIGINAL R10 000 — always R800/year. Under compound, each year's interest is calculated on the GROWING balance — so by year 2 the interest is calculated on R10 800, by year 3 on R11 664, and so on. Compound earns 'interest on interest', and that extra interest itself earns interest in later years, causing the gap to grow exponentially.
workingSteps: Identify that simple interest uses the SAME base every year.
Identify that compound uses a GROWING base.
Explain the snowball effect of interest-on-interest.

items.question: Sandile only plans to save for 2 years. Does it make a big difference whether he picks Account A or Account B?
items.expectedAnswer: Not really. A = 20 000 × 1,14 = R22 800. B = 20 000 × (1,07)^2 = R22 898. Difference is only R98 over 2 years. For short-term savings, simple vs compound makes very little difference; the gap only grows meaningfully over longer periods (5+ years).
workingSteps: Note that compound's advantage scales with time, not relevance for short-term savings.

stimulus.inline: **A young saver has R2 000 to invest. They can choose between two products: A pays 8% simple interest, B pays 7% compound interest.**

items.question: If they save for 10 years, which is better and by how much? Comment on what happens at very short time horizons.
items.expectedAnswer: After 10 years: A = R2 000 × 1,80 = R3 600. B = R2 000 × (1,07)^10 ≈ R3 934. Compound wins by R334 despite the lower rate, because compounding-interest-on-interest overtakes the higher simple rate. But at 1-2 years, the higher simple rate would beat compound at the lower rate. Compound only catches and overtakes after enough years for the snowball to outweigh the rate gap.
workingSteps: Show compound wins despite lower nominal rate.
Compare at short term (1 year: A = R2 160, B = R2 140) — simple wins.

stimulus.inline: **General principle: compound interest is better for savers, worse for borrowers (compared to simple at the same rate).**

items.question: Explain this principle in your own words.
items.expectedAnswer: For savers, compound interest works in your favour because each period's interest is added to the balance and itself earns interest in the next period — your money grows faster. For borrowers, the same mechanic works against you: any unpaid interest is added to what you owe, and you pay interest on that interest. So for someone receiving interest (a saver) compound is good; for someone paying interest (a borrower) compound makes the debt grow faster than simple interest would.
workingSteps: Identify who pays vs who receives interest.
Apply the snowball logic in both directions.

stimulus.inline: **A graph showing simple vs compound balances over 20 years for R10 000 at 7%.**

items.question: Which curve is the straight line, simple or compound? Why?
items.expectedAnswer: Simple interest is the straight line because the interest amount per year is constant (always 7% of the original R10 000 = R700). Constant growth = straight line. Compound interest is the upward-curving line because each year's interest is larger than the last (since it's calculated on a growing balance), and increasing growth = curve.
workingSteps: Identify which method gives constant per-period interest.
Link constant growth to straight line.

_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_COMPOUND_AS_SIMPLE: Calculates compound interest as if it were simple (or vice versa)
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_BALANCE_GROWTH_BASE: Calculates each period's compound interest on the wrong (typically the original P, not current) balance
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_TOTAL_VS_INTEREST: Reports total amount when asked for interest, or vice versa
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_SUBTRACTION_ORDER: Subtracts in the wrong order when computing the difference
